opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real risk, and honestly it's one the field has struggled with for a long time. Benchmarks are incredibly useful. They give everyone a shared target, they make progress legible, and a lot of the breakthroughs we've seen came from people rallying around a hard, well-defined problem. But the moment a benchmark becomes the thing you're optimizing for, it starts to lose its value as a measurement. That's basically Goodhart's law.

What I've seen is that there are a few different failure modes. The most obvious one is contamination, where the test data, or something very close to it, ends up in the training data, and you're measuring memorization rather than capability. But the subtler one is that even without any direct leakage, if you have hundreds of researchers making thousands of design decisions while staring at the same leaderboard, you end up implicitly overfitting. Each individual choice looks reasonable, but collectively you've tuned your system to that particular distribution of problems. Then you release the model, people try it on things that matter to them, and it doesn't feel as good as the numbers suggested.

The way I think about it is that benchmarks should be a proxy for something you actually care about, and you have to keep asking whether the proxy is still tracking the real thing. When I was working on poker, for example, the real test was playing against top professionals for real money over a large number of hands. You couldn't really game that. It was adversarial, it was out of distribution in the sense that the humans were adapting to you, and the result was very hard to argue with. I think that kind of evaluation is much more valuable than a static dataset.

So in practice, I'd say a few things. One, rotate your evaluations and keep some held out that nobody on the team optimizes against directly. Two, put a lot of weight on qualitative signal: what are people actually using the model for, where does it fail, does it feel smarter? Three, favor evaluations that are hard to saturate, like open-ended problems, or things where you're competing against strong humans or other systems. And four, be honest when a benchmark is effectively solved or saturated and move on rather than squeezing out the last percentage point.

The other thing I'd say is that the stakes are rising. When models were weaker, benchmark gaming mostly just meant a misleading paper. Now these numbers drive investment, deployment decisions, and even safety assessments. If we're fooling ourselves about capabilities, in either direction, that matters a lot more. So I think the field needs to invest much more seriously in evaluation as a discipline in its own right, rather than treating it as an afterthought to training.

r001.rationale: It recommends keeping evaluations held out so the team cannot optimize directly against them, which communicates using a private held-out evaluation to reduce benchmark overfitting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and honestly I think it's one of the bigger traps in the field right now.

The thing about benchmarks is that they're a proxy. They were created because somebody wanted to measure something real, like "can this model do math" or "can this model write code," and the benchmark is a snapshot of that capability at a particular moment. But the moment a benchmark becomes the target, it stops being a good proxy. That's basically Goodhart's law. And with AI it's even worse than in other fields, because the models are trained on the internet, and the benchmarks are on the internet, and so you get contamination even when nobody is trying to cheat. Then on top of that you have the explicit pressure, where a lab knows that a particular number is going to end up in a press release or a comparison table, and so people spend disproportionate effort on that number.

What I've seen is that the labs that are really good at this treat public benchmarks as a sanity check rather than an objective. The actual signal they care about is internal evals that nobody has seen, or just using the model yourself for the things you actually want it to do. When I was working on reasoning models, the test that mattered most to me wasn't a leaderboard, it was whether the model could do something it hadn't been able to do before, on problems I knew were clean. A benchmark can tell you you're moving in roughly the right direction. It can't tell you that you've actually gotten there.

The other risk, which I think is underappreciated, is that benchmarks shape what the field thinks is important. If everyone is measuring one thing, everyone builds toward that thing, and capabilities that don't have a convenient number attached to them get neglected. Some of the most important properties of these models, like whether they're reliable over a long task or whether they know when they don't know something, are much harder to put on a chart. So I'd say the risk isn't just that a model gets overfit to a benchmark. It's that the whole research agenda gets overfit to what's easy to measure.

That said, I don't want to be too negative. Benchmarks have been incredibly useful for the field. They give you a shared language and they make progress legible. I just think you have to hold them loosely, and you have to keep making new ones, because any benchmark that's been around for a while has probably already been saturated or compromised in some way.

r001.rationale: The response recommends internal evaluations that nobody has seen, but does not clearly say they should be held out from model optimization as a private evaluation set.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks are useful, but the risk is that you start treating the benchmark as the goal rather than as a measurement of something you actually care about. You want a model that can solve new problems, and a higher benchmark score doesn’t necessarily tell you that it’s better at doing that.

There’s the obvious issue of contamination: if the questions or solutions are in the training data, you’re not really measuring generalization. But there’s also a subtler issue where you make enough decisions based on a public benchmark that you effectively overfit to it, even without directly training on the answers.

So I’d want multiple sources of evidence, including held-out evaluations and performance on real tasks. If a benchmark improves, does that translate into the model being more useful? Can it handle a problem that somebody just came up with? That’s the capability we’re trying to build. The score is evidence about it, but it isn’t the capability itself.

r001.rationale: The response recommends held-out evaluations, but does not say the evaluation set should be private.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the risk is that you start confusing progress on the benchmark with progress on the underlying capability you care about. A benchmark is a proxy, and once everybody is optimizing against the same public set of questions, you can get better scores without getting a correspondingly more useful model.

That doesn’t necessarily mean somebody is deliberately training on the test set. You might try a hundred different approaches and keep the one that does best on that benchmark. Over time, you’re effectively fitting to it through your research decisions.

So I’d want to see whether the gains transfer to fresh problems, ideally problems that were created after the model was trained. Public benchmarks are useful, but I’d be cautious about treating a small difference on a leaderboard as strong evidence that one model is generally better.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking transfer to fresh problems, ideally created after training, but does not propose using a private held-out evaluation set.
